title: The Creation
hook: Three accounts of the Creation. Same event, three different vantage points—and the differences matter profoundly. Genesis gives us the physical cosmos taking shape. Moses reveals the spiritual pre-existence and the councils in heaven. Abraham pulls back the curtain further: 'They,' not 'He'—the Gods, plural, organizing what was already there. This isn't contradiction; it's stereoscopic vision. Each account adds dimension the others lack, and together they reveal something no other tradition possesses: the Creation wasn't a solo act of divine magic, but a collaborative council where intelligences, materials, and divine Beings worked together to prepare an earth where we could become like Them.
overview:
The Creation accounts span seven days—or rather, seven periods—of organized development, moving from light dividing darkness to the crowning creation of man and woman in the divine image. Genesis 1 presents the stately, liturgical rhythm: 'And God said... and it was so... and God saw that it was good.' Genesis 2 zooms in on the Garden, the formation of Adam from dust, the naming of animals, and the creation of Eve from Adam's side. But the real drama emerges when you layer Moses and Abraham over the Genesis text. Moses 2-3 restores critical theology: this earth has a spiritual creation preceding its physical one, there was a Grand Council, and Jehovah executed the Father's plan. The phrase 'I, God' replaces the distant third person, making clear that this is Christ's own account to Moses. Abraham 4-5 goes further: 'the Gods' organized and formed, using materials that pre-existed—'they watched those things which they had ordered.' This isn't creation ex nihilo but intelligent organization of eternal elements.

The theological architecture is stunning. Where Genesis says 'God created,' Moses clarifies 'I, God, created them spiritually' before physically. Where Genesis says Adam was formed from 'dust,' Moses adds he became 'a living soul'—a temple-worthy phrase that signals he received not just biological life but spiritual quickening. Eve isn't an afterthought but 'an help meet for him'—Hebrew 'ezer kenegdo,' a companion corresponding to him, his equal and counterpart. The rib account in Genesis 2:21-23 carries profound temple symbolism Latter-day Saints recognize: Eve comes from Adam's side while he sleeps, she is bone of his bone, and they become one flesh. The ancient Hebrew wordplay is lovely: Adam (ish) names her Woman (ishah) because she was taken from Man. This isn't biology; it's theology of eternal union.

The Restoration adds a third lens that transforms everything. The Book of Mormon teaches that 'all things denote there is a God; yea, even the earth, and all things that are upon the face of it' (Alma 30:44)—the Creation is not just history but sign and witness. The temple endowment walks patrons through Creation as the backdrop for understanding mortal purpose and divine covenants. Joseph Smith taught that the Hebrew word translated 'create' (bara) more accurately means 'to organize'—'God had materials to organize the world out of chaos—chaotic matter' (Teachings of the Prophet Joseph Smith, 350-352). This changes everything: we are not made from nothing but organized from intelligence and element, co-eternal with God. As Abraham 3:18 declares, 'If there be two spirits, and one shall be more intelligent than the other, yet these two spirits, notwithstanding one is more intelligent than the other, have no beginning; they existed before, they shall have no end.' We don't begin at birth; we existed in the pre-mortal councils Abraham witnessed.

The Creation accounts point to Christ at every turn. John 1:1-3 identifies Him as the Word through whom 'all things were made.' Moses 1:32-33 confirms He created 'worlds without number' under the Father's direction. Colossians 1:16 declares, 'by him were all things created... all things were created by him, and for him.' The six-day pattern culminating in sabbath rest prefigures Christ's mortal mission and millennial reign. Adam is 'the son of God' (Luke 3:38), a type of Christ, the Second Adam who will redeem what the first lost. The Garden becomes the inverse of Gethsemane: where Adam fell, Christ will atone. Every 'and God saw that it was good' anticipates the Father's witness at Christ's baptism: 'This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.' The Creation is Christocentric from before the foundations were laid.

These chapters also establish the pattern for all covenants. God speaks, names, blesses, commands, and rests—establishing divine order. Adam and Eve receive commandments, agency, and the possibility of growth through choice. The tree of knowledge isn't a trap but a threshold. Latter-day revelation clarifies what Genesis obscures: the Fall was foreordained, necessary, and in fact glorious. Lehi teaches, 'Adam fell that men might be; and men are, that they might have joy' (2 Nephi 2:25). The Creation sets the stage for the mortal experience: a probationary state where we exercise faith, make choices, and progress toward the divine image we already bear in embryonic form.

key_verses.text_kjv: And God said, Let us make man in our image, after our likeness: and let them have dominion over the fish of the sea, and over the fowl of the air, and over the cattle, and over all the earth, and over every creeping thing that creepeth upon the earth.
key_verses.insight: The plural 'us' and 'our' stumbles trinitarian theology but makes perfect sense in Restoration light: the Gods counsel together, and humanity is fashioned after the divine image—not metaphorically but literally, with potential to become as They are. 'Image' (tselem) and 'likeness' (demut) together suggest both physical form and divine nature.

key_verses.text_kjv: And God saw every thing that he had made, and, behold, it was very good. And the evening and the morning were the sixth day.
key_verses.insight: Six times God declared creation 'good' (tov), but only after humanity enters the scene does He declare it 'very good' (tov me'od). We are not an afterthought but the pinnacle and purpose. The material world isn't evil to escape but a divine gift for our progression.

key_verses.text_kjv: And I, God, said unto mine Only Begotten, which was with me from the beginning: Let us make man in our image, after our likeness; and it was so... And I, God, created man in mine own image, in the image of mine Only Begotten created I him; male and female created I them.
key_verses.insight: Moses restores what Genesis hints: the Father addresses the Son, the Only Begotten. Christ is not only present but the active agent of Creation. The image we bear is specifically the image of the Only Begotten, our Elder Brother, the prototype of the saved soul.

key_verses.text_kjv: And then the Lord said: Let us go down. And they went down at the beginning, and they, that is the Gods, organized and formed the heavens and the earth.
key_verses.insight: Abraham's plural 'Gods' (Elohim) and the verb 'organized' rather than 'created' revolutionize Creation theology. This is council language, temple language. The Gods descend—condescension is the pattern from the beginning—and organize pre-existing materials. Intelligence and element are co-eternal with God.

key_verses.text_kjv: Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife: and they shall be one flesh.
key_verses.insight: Quoted by Jesus in Matthew 19:5 as the divine standard for marriage, this verse establishes the primordial pattern: covenant union mirrors the Creation itself. The one-flesh union is physical, emotional, spiritual—and in temple theology, eternal. Adam and Eve model the sealing covenant that predates the Fall.

highlights.snippet_text: The Hebrew 'Elohim' is plural—Gods—but paired with a singular verb 'created' (bara). This grammatical peculiarity has puzzled Jewish scholars for millennia. The Restoration resolves it: the Godhead acts in perfect unity, and Abraham later shows us the plural is literal—multiple divine Beings organized the earth under the Father's direction.
highlights.label: Hebrew

highlights.snippet_text: Moses clarifies what Genesis omits: 'For I, the Lord God, created all things... spiritually, before they were naturally upon the face of the earth.' Everything existed in spirit form first. This dual creation—spiritual then physical—maps perfectly onto the doctrine of pre-mortal existence and the necessity of mortality for progression.
highlights.label: Restoration

highlights.snippet_text: Abraham witnesses the Grand Council before the Creation: 'The Lord said... We will go down... and we will prove them herewith.' The Creation accounts are the execution of this pre-mortal council decision. The same intelligences present there—including us—are now experiencing the probation that council planned.
highlights.label: Cross-Ref

highlights.snippet_text: Ancient Near Eastern texts often depict gods creating humans to serve as slaves. Genesis radically inverts this: Adam becomes 'a living soul' (nephesh chayyah), the same phrase used for animals in Genesis 1:21—but humanity receives the divine image and dominion. We are not divine servants but divine children.
highlights.label: Historical

highlights.snippet_text: Eve coming from Adam's side while he sleeps, then becoming his wife, carries profound temple symbolism. President Spencer W. Kimball taught that Adam's sleep was 'a deep sleep' like a trance or vision, and that Eve's creation was likely more sublime than the rib account suggests. The endowment ceremony presents this event as sacred instruction, not biology lesson.
highlights.label: Restoration

highlights.snippet_text: Joseph Smith taught, 'The head God called together the Gods and sat in grand council to bring forth the world' (King Follett Discourse). Abraham chapter 4 is the closest scriptural account of that council. This isn't Mormon folklore—it's canonized scripture revealing the plural divine council pattern found throughout the Old Testament.
highlights.label: Prophetic

restoration_lens:
The Joseph Smith Translation and the books of Moses and Abraham transform the Creation from a children's story into profound theology. The JST doesn't just polish Genesis—it restores entire theological frameworks Genesis lost or never contained. Moses 1:33-39 adds the stunning revelation that the earth is 'only one of countless worlds' Christ created for the Father's purposes: 'to bring to pass the immortality and eternal life of man.' The Creation isn't God's hobby—it's the mechanics of exaltation. Moses 2:1 clarifies that 'I, God, created' refers to Christ acting under the Father's direction, resolving the identity question. Moses 3:4-7 reveals the dual creation—spiritual before physical—giving doctrinal foundation for the pre-mortal existence taught in Abraham 3. The Doctrine and Covenants adds its witness: Section 76 shows us the pre-mortal council; Section 88 calls the earth itself 'sanctified' and destined for celestial glory; Section 93 declares Christ is the 'light and life of the world,' the same light that divided darkness on day one.

Abraham 4-5 gives the most detailed account of divine plurality in our canon. The language shifts from Genesis's Elohim with singular verbs to 'the Gods' with plural verbs throughout: 'they organized,' 'they said,' 'they watched.' This isn't polytheism—it's the plurality of the Godhead and the council pattern. Abraham 3 precedes the Creation chapters deliberately, showing us the pre-mortal realm where intelligences already existed, where we were among 'the noble and great ones,' where Christ was chosen as Redeemer before the foundation of the world. The Creation accounts are the execution phase of a pre-mortal plan. When Abraham 4:26 records the Gods saying 'Let us make man in our image,' Abraham the prophet has already seen who 'us' and 'our' refer to—he witnessed the council. The temple endowment walks us through the Creation as prelude to the Fall and Atonement precisely because these events form one continuous narrative of divine love and human potential.

Modern prophets have consistently taught that the Creation accounts are symbolic as well as historical. Elder Bruce R. McConkie wrote, 'These accounts are speaking to us in the language of symbolism, a language that is plainer and more expressive than any other' (The Millennial Messiah). President Joseph Fielding Smith taught that the 'days' of Creation were likely vast periods: 'The Lord has never revealed to us the precise time when the earth was created... we are not bound to the idea that the days were periods of twenty-four hours' (Man: His Origin and Destiny). The point isn't that Genesis is untrue but that it's compressing deep time and profound theology into symbolic narrative. The Restoration lens doesn't diminish Genesis—it enlarges it, adding the spiritual dimension, the pre-mortal context, and the eternal trajectory: we existed before, we are here to be proven, and we have the potential to become as our Creators are.
application:
For covenant members navigating a secular world that reduces the Creation to either fundamentalist literalism or Darwinian accident, these chapters offer a third way: purposeful, intelligent organization of eternal materials by divine Beings who are our literal Parents, preparing a stage for our eternal progression. The Creation accounts aren't about when or how in mechanical terms—they're about why and who. Why does anything exist? Because eternal Parents wanted children who could grow to become like Them. Who made it? Christ, under the Father's direction, in council with the great and noble ones. The question isn't whether you believe in a young earth or an old earth but whether you see your own divine origin in these verses. You are not an accident of chemistry. You are organized intelligence, given a body, placed in a world designed for your growth, with a Redeemer prepared from before its foundation. That changes how you see everything.

For parents, especially, these chapters are foundational. When you teach your children about the Creation, you're not giving them science—you're giving them identity. 'In the image of God created he him; male and female created he them.' Your daughter needs to know she bears the image of Heavenly Mother and Heavenly Father alike. Your son needs to know dominion over the earth means stewardship, not exploitation—we are gardeners, not conquerors. When Genesis says Adam named the animals, it's showing us that humanity participates in creation itself, bringing order and meaning. When Eve is called 'an help meet for him,' the Hebrew ezer kenegdo means a rescuer, a strength, a necessary counterpart—she is not subordinate but essential. Teach your children that marriage is patterned after the Creation itself: 'Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife: and they shall be one flesh.' This is covenant language, temple language. It's not just romantic—it's cosmic.

For individuals facing doubt or deconstruction, these chapters are an anchor. The world says you're the product of blind forces, that consciousness is an illusion, that meaning is constructed. The Creation accounts declare the opposite: You are a child of God, fashioned in Their image, endowed with agency, given this earth as the arena for your progression toward exaltation. The material world is not evil, not a trap—it's a divine gift. Your body is not a prison but a temple. The struggles of mortality are not punishment but curriculum. And the Savior who organized this world atom by atom knows you intimately and has prepared the way for you to return. When Abraham saw the Grand Council and heard the plan, he tells us that 'the Lord said: Whom shall I send? And one answered like unto the Son of Man: Here am I, send me' (Abraham 3:27). Christ volunteered. He chose to be your Redeemer before you took your first breath. The Creation accounts are His love letter written in light, land, and life.
